== Strong field tests ==
The very strong gravitational fields that are present close to [[black hole]]s, especially those [[supermassive black hole]]s which are thought to power [[active galactic nuclei]] and the more active [[quasar]]s, belong to a field of intense active research. Observations of these quasars and active galactic nuclei are difficult, and interpretation of the observations is heavily dependent upon astrophysical models other than general relativity or competing fundamental [[Alternatives to general relativity|theories of gravitation]], but they are qualitatively consistent with the black hole concept as modeled in general relativity.

=== Binary pulsars ===
{{further|Binary pulsar}}
[[Pulsars]] are rapidly rotating [[neutron star]]s which emit regular radio pulses as they rotate. As such they act as clocks which allow very precise monitoring of their orbital motions.  Due to their strong gravitational fields, short period orbits, and high orbital speeds, relativistic effects are much larger and easier to measure in pulsar data than they are in the solar system. These effects can then be compared to the predictions of general relativity.<ref name="Freire2024"/> 

Relativistic effects visible in pulsar orbits include:<ref name="Freire2024"/>
* Orbital period changes due to gravitational radiation.  The rate of orbital period change is denoted as <math>\dot{P}_{orb}</math>.
* [[Periapsis]] precession, measured as <math>\dot{\omega}</math>.  In the solar system, this maxes out at arcseconds/century.  In binary pulsars it can be tens of degrees per year.
* Changes in clock rates, parameterized by <math>\gamma</math>, from going in and out of gravity wells.
* Delay in propagation of light as it passes near a massive object, or [[Shapiro time delay]], parameterized as ''r'' and ''s''.
General relativity predicts a specific value for each such parameter.  If a measured value differs from this by more than experimental error, general relativity could not be correct.  All such measurements are consistent with general relativity.<ref name="Freire2024"/>

For example, observations of pulsars in orbit around other stars have all demonstrated substantial [[periapsis]] precessions that cannot be accounted for classically but can be accounted for by using general relativity. As one example, the Hulse–Taylor [[binary pulsar]] [[PSR B1913+16]] (a pair of neutron stars in which one is detected as a pulsar) has an observed precession of over 4° of arc per year (periastron shift per orbit only about 10<sup>−6</sup>). This precession, in combination with other relativistic effects, has been used to compute the masses of the components of this and other binary pulsars.

In general relativity, a gravitating mass that is in [[quadrupole]] or higher order vibration, or is asymmetric and in rotation, must emit gravitational waves.<ref>In general relativity, a perfectly spherical star (in vacuum) that expands or contracts while remaining perfectly spherical ''cannot'' emit any gravitational waves (similar to the lack of e/m radiation from a pulsating charge), as [[Birkhoff's theorem (relativity)|Birkhoff's theorem]] says that the geometry remains the same exterior to the star. More generally, a rotating system will only emit gravitational waves if it lacks the axial symmetry with respect to the axis of rotation.</ref>  For example, planets orbiting the Sun, or binary stars in orbit around each other, constantly lose energy via gravitational radiation.  In the solar system this effect is effect is so small it cannot be measured - for example, the Earth's orbital period decreases by about 1 part in <math>3\times 10^{23}</math> per year due to [[gravitational wave|gravitational radiation]],{{efn|The [[Two-body problem in general relativity#Gravitational radiation|Gravitational radiation]] from an assumed circular orbit is <math>\frac{32}{5}\frac{G^4}{c^5}\frac{(M_{\odot}M_{\oplus})^2(M_{\odot}+M_{\oplus})}{r^5}</math>, or about 200 watts for Earth.  In contrast the Earth's kinetic energy is about <math>\frac{GM_{\odot}M_{\oplus}}{2r}</math>, or about 3x10<sup>33</sup> joules by classical mechanics.  This energy loss leads to the orbital period shrinking by about 10<sup>-16</sup> seconds per year.}} far too small to be currently measured.  In binary pulsar systems, the effect is much more measurable, with the equivalent energy loss driving a visible change in the orbital period.

This radiation of gravitational waves has been inferred from the [[PSR B1913+16|Hulse–Taylor binary]] (and other binary pulsars).<ref>{{cite journal|last=Stairs|first=Ingrid H.|title=Testing General Relativity with Pulsar Timing|journal=Living Reviews in Relativity|volume=6|issue=1|article-number=5|doi=10.12942/lrr-2003-5|pmid=28163640|pmc=5253800|arxiv = astro-ph/0307536 |bibcode = 2003LRR.....6....5S |year=2003|doi-access=free }}</ref> Precise timing of the pulses shows that the stars orbit only approximately according to [[Kepler's Laws]]: over time they gradually spiral towards each other, demonstrating an [[energy]] loss in close agreement with the predicted energy radiated by gravitational waves.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Weisberg | first1= J. M. | date= October 1981| title=Gravitational waves from an orbiting pulsar | journal=Scientific American | volume = 245 | issue= 4 | pages=74–82 |  doi=10.1038/scientificamerican1081-74 | bibcode=1981SciAm.245d..74W | last2 = Taylor | first2 = J. H. | last3 = Fowler | first3 = L. A. }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1=Weisberg | first1= J. M. | date=  2010| title=Timing Measurements of the Relativistic Binary Pulsar PSR B1913+16 | journal=Astrophysical Journal | volume = 722 | issue= 2 | pages=1030–1034 | doi=10.1088/0004-637X/722/2/1030 | arxiv =  	1011.0718 | bibcode=2010ApJ...722.1030W | last3 = Taylor | first3 = J. H. | last2 = Nice | first2 = D. J. | s2cid= 118573183 }}</ref> For their discovery of the first binary pulsar and measuring its orbital decay due to gravitational-wave emission, [[Russell Alan Hulse|Hulse]] and [[Joseph Hooton Taylor, Jr.|Taylor]] won the 1993 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Press Release: The Nobel Prize in Physics 1993|url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/1993/press.html|publisher=[[Nobel Prize]]|access-date=6 May 2014|date=13 October 1993}}</ref>

[[File:DoublePulsarRelativityTest.png|thumb|The mass–mass diagram for the PSR J1856–0039 DNS system. The three colored curves show the dependency of post-Keplerian parameters <math>\dot{\omega}</math> (rate of [[periastron]] advance), <math>\dot{P}_{orb}</math> (rate of change of [[orbital period]]), and <math>\gamma</math> (Einstein delay). The inset enlarges the area where all three curves meet, confirming GR is sufficient to predict these PK parameters. The mass function for this binary disallows the gray region of combined masses.<ref name=Yang-2006/>]]

A "double pulsar" discovered in 2003, [[PSR J0737-3039]], has a periastron precession of 16.90° per year; unlike the Hulse–Taylor binary, both [[neutron star]]s are detected as pulsars, allowing precision timing of both members of the system. Due to this, the tight orbit, the fact that the system is almost edge-on, and the very low transverse velocity of the system as seen from Earth, J0737−3039 and similar systems provide stringent strong-field tests of general relativity.  At least five distinct relativistic effects can be observed, including orbital decay as in the Hulse–Taylor system. The relativitic effects can be described as so-called ''post-Keplerian'' (PK) parameters, each of which depends on the masses of the two objects in different ways. From the point of intersection of any two parameters in the <math>M_1-M_2</math> plane, both masses can be determined. General relativity further predicts all of the parameter curves will intersect at one point, making the size of the common intersection region of three or more curves a test of the theory.<ref name="Freire2024">{{Cite journal |last=Freire |first=Paulo C. C. |last2=Wex |first2=Norbert |date=July 22, 2024 |title=Gravity experiments with radio pulsars |url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/s41114-024-00051-y |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=5 |doi=10.1007/s41114-024-00051-y |issn=1433-8351}}</ref>

An example of such a test is shown in the figure.<ref name=Yang-2006>{{Cite journal 
 | last1 = Yang | first1 = Z. L. 
 | last2 = Han | first2 = J. L. 
 | last3 = Su | first3 = W. Q. 
 | last4 = Wang | first4 = P. F. 
 | last5 = Wang | first5 = C. 
 | last6 = Wang | first6 = T. 
 | last7 = Zhou | first7 = D. J. 
 | last8 = Yan | first8 = Yi 
 | last9 = Xu | first9 = J. 
 | display-authors = etal 
 | date = 15 September 2026 
 | title = Relativistic Effects of PSR J1856–0039 Double Neutron Star System in a 2.36-Hour Compact Orbit 
 | journal = Physical Review Letters 
 | volume = 137 
 | pages = 121401 
 | doi = 10.1103/hmjp-htd1 
 | url = https://journals.aps.org/prl/abstract/10.1103/hmjp-htd1
}}</ref>. If GR is the correct, then all curves will intersect in one small region, within the margin of error of measurement.  Here, three relativistic estimates are shown as a function of M1 and M2. 

After observing the system J0737-3039 for two and a half years, four independent tests of general relativity were possible, the most precise (the Shapiro delay) confirming the general relativity prediction within 0.05%<ref>{{cite journal | author = Kramer, M. | title = Tests of general relativity from timing the double pulsar | journal = Science |volume = 314 | date = 2006 | pages = 97–102 | doi = 10.1126/science.1132305 | pmid = 16973838 | issue = 5796|arxiv = astro-ph/0609417 |bibcode = 2006Sci...314...97K | display-authors = 1 | last2 = Stairs | first2 = I. H. | last3 = Manchester | first3 = R. N. | last4 = McLaughlin | first4 = M. A. | last5 = Lyne | first5 = A. G. | last6 = Ferdman | first6 = R. D. | last7 = Burgay | first7 = M. | last8 = Lorimer | first8 = D. R. | last9 = Possenti | first9 = A. | s2cid = 6674714 }}</ref> (nevertheless the periastron shift per orbit is only about 0.0013% of a circle and thus it is not a higher-order relativity test).

Tests of general relativity have been extended to neutron stars with masses of {{val|2|u=solar mass}} by studying the pulsar-white dwarf system [[PSR J0348+0432]].<ref>{{cite journal | author =Antoniadis, John | display-authors =etal |title=A Massive Pulsar in a Compact Relativistic Binary |doi=10.1126/science.1233232 |arxiv=1304.6875 |journal=Science |volume=340 |issue=6131 |date=2013 |bibcode = 2013Sci...340..448A |article-number=1233232 |pmid=23620056| s2cid =15221098 }}</ref> These tests eliminate many but not all alternative theories.<ref>{{cite journal |url=http://www.nature.com/news/massive-double-star-is-latest-test-for-einstein-s-gravity-theory-1.12880#/b1 |title=Massive double star is latest test for Einstein's gravity theory |date=25 April 2013 |journal=  Nature|access-date=7 May 2013 |doi=10.1038/nature.2013.12880 |last1=Cowen |first1=Ron |s2cid=123752543 }}</ref>

=== Direct detection of gravitational waves ===
A number of [[gravitational-wave observatory|gravitational-wave detector]]s have been built with the intent of directly detecting the gravitational waves emanating from such astronomical events as the merger of two [[neutron star]]s or [[black hole]]s. In February 2016, the [[Advanced LIGO]] team announced that they had [[gravitational-wave detection|directly detected gravitational waves]] from a stellar [[binary black hole]] merger,<ref name="Discovery 2016">{{cite journal |title=Einstein's gravitational waves found at last |journal=Nature News|url=http://www.nature.com/news/einstein-s-gravitational-waves-found-at-last-1.19361 |date=February 11, 2016 |last1=Castelvecchi |first1=Davide |last2=Witze |first2=Witze |doi=10.1038/nature.2016.19361  |s2cid=182916902|access-date=2016-02-11 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Observation of Gravitational Waves from a Binary Black Hole Merger|author=B. P. Abbott |display-authors=etal | journal=Physical Review Letters| year=2016| volume=116|issue=6| doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.061102| pmid=26918975| article-number=061102| arxiv=1602.03837| bibcode=2016PhRvL.116f1102A|s2cid=124959784 }}</ref><ref name=NSF>{{Cite web|title = Gravitational waves detected 100 years after Einstein's prediction {{!}} NSF - National Science Foundation|url = https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=137628|website = www.nsf.gov|access-date = 2016-02-11|archive-date = 2020-06-19|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20200619020139/https://www.nsf.gov/news/news_summ.jsp?cntn_id=137628}}</ref> with additional detections announced in June 2016, June 2017, and August 2017.<ref name="conover2017" /><ref>{{cite web|last1=Choi|first1=Charles Q.|title=Gravitational Waves Detected from Neutron-Star Crashes: The Discovery Explained|url=https://www.space.com/38471-gravitational-waves-neutron-star-crashes-discovery-explained.html|website=Space.com|date=16 October 2017|publisher=Purch|access-date=1 November 2017}}</ref>

General relativity predicts gravitational waves, as does any theory of gravitation in which changes in the gravitational field propagate at a finite speed.<ref>{{cite journal| last=Schutz|first=Bernard F.| title=Gravitational waves on the back of an envelope|journal=American Journal of Physics| volume=52| issue=5| pages=412–419|doi=10.1119/1.13627|bibcode = 1984AmJPh..52..412S |hdl=11858/00-001M-0000-0013-747D-5|url=http://pubman.mpdl.mpg.de/pubman/item/escidoc:52023/component/escidoc:52024/60304.pdf|year=1984|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Then, the LIGO response function could discriminate among the various theories.<ref>{{Cite book|last=R.|first=Saulson, Peter|title=Fundamentals of interferometric gravitational wave detectors|date=1994|publisher=World scientific|isbn=981-02-1820-6|oclc=799449990}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Corda|first=Christian|date=2009-12-31|title=Interferometric detection of gravitational waves: the definitive test for general relativity|url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0218271809015904|journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D|volume=18|issue=14|pages=2275–2282|doi=10.1142/S0218271809015904|issn=0218-2718|arxiv=0905.2502|bibcode=2009IJMPD..18.2275C|s2cid=721314}}</ref> Since gravitational waves can be directly detected,<ref name="Discovery 2016"/><ref name=NSF/> it is possible to use them to learn about the Universe. This is [[gravitational-wave astronomy]]. Gravitational-wave astronomy can test general relativity by verifying that the observed waves are of the form predicted (for example, that they only have two transverse polarizations), and by checking that [[black hole]]s are the objects described by solutions of the [[Einstein field equations]].<ref>{{cite journal| last=Gair|first=Jonathan|author2=Vallisneri, Michele |author3=Larson, Shane L. |author4= Baker, John G. |title=Testing General Relativity with Low-Frequency, Space-Based Gravitational-Wave Detectors| journal=Living Reviews in Relativity| volume=16|issue=1|page=7| doi=10.12942/lrr-2013-7|pmid=28163624|pmc=5255528| arxiv = 1212.5575 |bibcode = 2013LRR....16....7G |year=2013|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal| last=Yunes|first=Nicolás|author2-link=Xavier Siemens|author2=Siemens, Xavier |title=Gravitational-Wave Tests of General Relativity with Ground-Based Detectors and Pulsar-Timing Arrays|journal=Living Reviews in Relativity| volume=16|issue=1|page=9|doi=10.12942/lrr-2013-9|pmid=28179845|pmc=5255575|arxiv = 1304.3473 |bibcode = 2013LRR....16....9Y |year=2013|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="tests">{{cite journal |journal=Physical Review Letters |volume=116 |issue=221101|article-number=221101 |year=2016 |title=Tests of general relativity with GW150914 |collaboration=LIGO Scientific Collaboration and Virgo Collaboration |last1=Abbott |first1=Benjamin P. |url= http://strathprints.strath.ac.uk/56932/ |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.116.221101 |pmid=27314708 |bibcode=2016PhRvL.116v1101A|arxiv=1602.03841 |s2cid=217275338 }}</ref>

Gravitational-wave astronomy can also test Maxwell-Einstein field equations. This version of the field equations predicts that spinning magnetars (i.e., neutron stars with extremely strong magnetic dipole field) should emit gravitational waves.<ref>{{Cite journal|arxiv=0907.2290|first1=A.|last1=Corsi|author1-link=Alessandra Corsi|first2=P.|last2=Meszaros|title=GRB Afterglow Plateaus and gravitational waves: multi-messenger signature of a millisecond Magnetar?|journal=Astrophys. J.|volume=702|pages=1171–1178|date=8 Nov 2018|doi=10.1088/0004-637X/702/2/1171|s2cid=16723637}}</ref>

"These amazing observations are the confirmation of a lot of theoretical work, including Einstein's general theory of relativity, which predicts gravitational waves", said Stephen Hawking.<ref name="Discovery 2016"/>

=== Direct observation of black holes ===
[[File:Black hole - Messier 87 crop max res.jpg|thumb|right|350px|A bright ring of material surrounding a dark center that marks the shadow of the M87's [[supermassive black hole]]. The image also provided a key confirmation of General relativity.<ref name="First M87 EHT"/>]]
The galaxy M87 was the subject of observation by the [[Event Horizon Telescope]] (EHT) in 2017; the 10 April 2019 issue of ''[[Astrophysical Journal Letters]]'' (vol. 875, No. 1) was dedicated to the EHT results, publishing six [[open-access]] papers. The [[event horizon]] of the black hole at the center of M87 was directly imaged at the wavelength of radio waves by the EHT; the image was revealed in a press conference on 10 April 2019, the first image of a black hole's event horizon.<ref>{{cite news|title=Focus on the First Event Horizon Telescope Results|work=Shep Doeleman|publisher=[[The Astrophysical Journal]]|date=10 April 2019|url=https://iopscience.iop.org/journal/2041-8205/page/Focus_on_EHT|access-date=14 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="First M87 EHT">{{cite journal|title=First M87 Event Horizon Telescope Results. I. The Shadow of the Supermassive Black Hole|author=The Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration |journal=The Astrophysical Journal|issue=1|pages=L1 |volume=875|doi=10.3847/2041-8213/ab0ec7|year=2019 |bibcode=2019ApJ...875L...1E |arxiv=1906.11238 |s2cid=145906806 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
In May 2022, the EHT provided the first image of the super massive black hole Sagittarius A* in the center of our own Milky Way galaxy.

=== Gravitational redshift and orbit precession of star in strong gravity field ===
Gravitational redshift in light from the [[S2 (star)|S2]] star orbiting the supermassive black hole [[Sagittarius A*]] in the center of the Milky Way has been measured with the [[Very Large Telescope]] using GRAVITY, NACO and SIFONI instruments.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.mpe.mpg.de/6930756/news20180726|title=First Successful Test of Einstein's General Relativity Near Supermassive Black Hole|publisher=[[Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics]]|work=Hämmerle, Hannelore|date=26 July 2018|access-date=28 July 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Detection of the gravitational redshift in the orbit of the star S2 near the Galactic centre massive black hole|author=GRAVITY Collaboration|date=26 July 2018|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|volume=615|issue=L15|pages=L15|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201833718|doi-access=free|arxiv=1807.09409|bibcode=2018A&A...615L..15G|s2cid=118891445}}</ref> Additionally, there has now been detection of the Schwarzschild precession in the orbit of the star S2 near the Galactic centre massive black hole.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Detection of the Schwarzschild precession in the orbit of the star S2 near the Galactic centre massive black hole|author=GRAVITY Collaboration|date=16 April 2020|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|volume=636|issue=L5|pages=L5|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/202037813|doi-access=free|arxiv=2004.07187|bibcode=2020A&A...636L...5G|s2cid=215768928}}</ref>

=== Strong equivalence principle ===
The strong equivalence principle of general relativity requires universality of free fall to apply even to bodies with strong self-gravity. Direct tests of this principle using Solar System bodies are limited by the weak self-gravity of the bodies, and tests using pulsar–white-dwarf binaries have been limited by the weak gravitational pull of the Milky Way. With the discovery of a triple star system called [[PSR J0337+1715]], located about 4,200 light-years from Earth, the strong equivalence principle can be tested with a high accuracy. This system contains a [[neutron star]] in a 1.6-day orbit with a [[white dwarf]] star, and the pair in a 327-day orbit with another white dwarf further away. This system permits a test that compares how the gravitational pull of the outer white dwarf affects the pulsar, which has strong self-gravity, and the inner white dwarf. The result shows that the accelerations of the pulsar and its nearby white-dwarf companion differ fractionally by no more than 2.6{{e|−6}} (95% [[Confidence interval|confidence level]]).<ref>{{cite journal|title=Universality of free fall from the orbital motion of a pulsar in a stellar triple system|author=Anne M. Archibald |author-link=Anne Archibald|display-authors=etal |journal=Nature|volume=559|issue=7712 |pages=73–76|date=4 July 2018|doi=10.1038/s41586-018-0265-1|arxiv=1807.02059 |bibcode=2018Natur.559...73A |pmid=29973733|s2cid=49578025 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Even Phenomenally Dense Neutron Stars Fall like a Feather - Einstein Gets It Right Again|url=https://public.nrao.edu/news/neutron-stars-fall/|publisher=NRAO|date=4 July 2018|access-date=28 July 2018|work=Charles Blue, Paul Vosteen}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Voisin|first1=G.|last2=Cognard|first2=I.|last3=Freire|first3=P. C. C.|last4=Wex|first4=N.|last5=Guillemot|first5=L.|last6=Desvignes|first6=G.|last7=Kramer|first7=M.|last8=Theureau|first8=G.|date=2020-06-01|title=An improved test of the strong equivalence principle with the pulsar in a triple star system|url=https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/abs/2020/06/aa38104-20/aa38104-20.html|journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics|language=en|volume=638|pages=A24|arxiv=2005.01388|doi=10.1051/0004-6361/202038104|doi-access=free|bibcode=2020A&A...638A..24V|s2cid=218486794|issn=0004-6361}}</ref>

=== X-ray spectroscopy ===
This technique is based on the idea that [[Geodesics in general relativity|photon trajectories]] are modified in the presence of a gravitational body. A very common astrophysical system in the universe is a [[black hole]] surrounded by an [[accretion disk]]. The radiation from the general neighborhood, including the accretion disk, is affected by the nature of the central black hole. Assuming Einstein's theory is correct, astrophysical black holes are described by the Kerr metric. (A consequence of the [[no-hair theorem]]s.) Thus, by analyzing the radiation from such systems, it is possible to test Einstein's theory.

Most of the radiation from these black hole – accretion disk systems (e.g., [[X-ray binary|black hole binaries]] and [[Active galactic nucleus|active galactic nuclei]]) arrives in the form of X-rays. When modeled, the radiation is decomposed into several components. Tests of Einstein's theory are possible with the thermal spectrum (only for black hole binaries) and the [[reflection spectrum#High-energy astrophysics|reflection spectrum]] (for both black hole binaries and active galactic nuclei). The former is not expected to provide strong constraints,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Kong|first1=Lingyao|last2=Li|first2=Zilong|last3=Bambi|first3=Cosimo|date=2014|title=Constraints on the Spacetime Geometry around 10 Stellar-mass Black Hole Candidates from the Disk's Thermal Spectrum|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|language=en|volume=797|issue=2|page=78|doi=10.1088/0004-637X/797/2/78|issn=0004-637X|arxiv=1405.1508|bibcode=2014ApJ...797...78K|s2cid=119280889}}</ref> while the latter is much more promising.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bambi|first=Cosimo|date=2017-04-06|title=Testing black hole candidates with electromagnetic radiation|journal=Reviews of Modern Physics|volume=89|issue=2|article-number=025001|doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.89.025001|arxiv=1509.03884|bibcode=2017RvMP...89b5001B|s2cid=118397255}}</ref> In both cases, systematic uncertainties might make such tests more challenging.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Krawczynski|first=Henric|date=2018-07-24|title=Difficulties of quantitative tests of the Kerr-hypothesis with X-ray observations of mass accreting black holes|journal=General Relativity and Gravitation|language=en|volume=50|issue=8|article-number=100|doi=10.1007/s10714-018-2419-8|issn=0001-7701|arxiv=1806.10347|bibcode=2018GReGr..50..100K|s2cid=119372075}}</ref>

== Cosmological tests ==
Tests of general relativity on the largest scales are not nearly so stringent as Solar System tests.<ref>{{cite book | author = Peebles, P. J. E.| title= General Relativity and Gravitation | chapter= Probing General Relativity on the Scales of Cosmology | date= December 2004 | arxiv= astro-ph/0410284|bibcode = 2005grg..conf..106P |doi = 10.1142/9789812701688_0010 | isbn = 978-981-256-424-5 | pages = 106–117 | s2cid= 1700265}}</ref> The earliest such test was the prediction and discovery of the [[expansion of the universe]].<ref name=Rudnicki28/> In 1922, [[Alexander Friedmann]] found that the Einstein equations have non-stationary solutions (even in the presence of the [[cosmological constant]]).<ref name=Pauli1/><ref>[[#Kragh|Kragh]], 2003, p. 152</ref> In 1927, [[Georges Lemaître]] showed that static solutions of the Einstein equations, which are possible in the presence of the cosmological constant, are unstable, and therefore the static universe envisioned by Einstein could not exist (it must either expand or contract).<ref name=Pauli1>[[#Pauli|W.Pauli]], 1958, pp. 219–220</ref> Lemaître made an explicit prediction that the universe should expand.<ref name="Kragh, 2003, p. 153">[[#Kragh|Kragh]], 2003, p. 153</ref> He also derived a redshift-distance relationship, which is now known as the [[Hubble Law]].<ref name="Kragh, 2003, p. 153"/> Later, in 1931, Einstein himself agreed with the results of Friedmann and Lemaître.<ref name=Pauli1/> The expansion of the universe discovered by [[Edwin Hubble]] in 1929<ref name=Pauli1/> was then considered by many (and continues to be considered by some now) as a direct confirmation of general relativity.<ref>[[#Rudnicki|Rudnicki]], 1991, p. 28</ref> In the 1930s, largely due to the work of [[Edward Arthur Milne]], it was realised that the linear relationship between redshift and distance derives from the general assumption of uniformity and isotropy rather than specifically from general relativity.<ref name=Rudnicki28>[[#Rudnicki|Rudnicki]], 1991, p. 28. ''The Hubble Law was viewed by many as an observational confirmation of General Relativity in the early years''</ref> However the prediction of a non-static universe was non-trivial, indeed dramatic, and primarily motivated by general relativity.<ref>[[#Chandrasekhar|Chandrasekhar]], 1980, p. 37</ref>

Some other cosmological tests include searches for primordial gravitational waves generated during [[cosmic inflation]], which may be detected in the [[cosmic microwave background]] [[Polarization (waves)|polarization]]<ref>{{cite journal|title=Cosmology: The test of inflation|author=Hand, Eric|journal=Nature|date=2009|volume=458|issue=7240|pages=820–824|doi=10.1038/458820a|pmid=19370005|doi-access=free}}</ref> or by a proposed space-based [[gravitational-wave detector|gravitational-wave interferometer]] called the [[Big Bang Observer]]. Other tests at high redshift are constraints on other theories of gravity,<ref>{{cite journal|title=Confirmation of general relativity on large scales from weak lensing and galaxy velocities|author=Reyes, Reinabelle|display-authors=etal|journal=Nature|date=2010|volume=464|issue=7286|pages=256–258|doi=10.1038/nature08857|arxiv = 1003.2185 |bibcode = 2010Natur.464..256R|pmid=20220843|s2cid=205219902}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=A test of the nature of cosmic acceleration using galaxy redshift distortions|author=Guzzo, L.|display-authors=etal|journal=Nature|date=2008|volume=451|issue=7178|pages=541–544|doi=10.1038/nature06555|arxiv = 0802.1944 |bibcode = 2008Natur.451..541G|pmid=18235494|s2cid=4403989}}</ref> and the variation of the gravitational constant since [[Big Bang nucleosynthesis]] (it varied by no more than 40% since then).{{citation needed|date=July 2012}}

In August 2017, the findings of tests conducted by astronomers using the [[European Southern Observatory]]'s [[Very Large Telescope]] (VLT), among other instruments, were released, and positively demonstrated gravitational effects predicted by Albert Einstein. One of these tests observed the orbit of the stars circling around [[Sagittarius A*]], a black hole about 4 million times as massive as the sun. Einstein's theory suggested that large objects bend the space around them, causing other objects to diverge from the straight lines they would otherwise follow. Although previous studies have validated Einstein's theory, this was the first time his theory had been tested on such a gigantic object. The findings were published in ''[[The Astrophysical Journal]]''.<ref name="Einstein-TheoryOfRelativity">{{cite news |last=Patel |first=Neel V. |title=The Milky Way's Supermassive Black Hole is Proving Einstein Correct |language=en |publisher=Inverse via Yahoo.news |date=9 August 2017 |url=https://www.yahoo.com/news/milky-way-supermassive-black-hole-121900474.html |access-date=9 August 2017 }}</ref><ref name="SeanDuffy2017">{{cite news |last=Duffy |first=Sean |title=Black Hole Indicates Einstein Was Right: Gravity Bends Space |language=en |publisher=Courthouse News Service |date=10 August 2017 |url=https://www.courthousenews.com/black-hole-indicates-einstein-right-gravity-bends-space/ |access-date=10 August 2017}}</ref>

=== Gravitational lensing ===
Astronomers using the Hubble Space Telescope and the Very Large Telescope have made precise tests of general relativity on galactic scales. The nearby galaxy [[ESO 325-G004]] acts as a strong gravitational lens, distorting light from a distant galaxy behind it to create an [[Einstein ring]] around its centre. By comparing the mass of ESO 325-G004 (from measurements of the motions of stars inside this galaxy) with the curvature of space around it, astronomers found that gravity behaves as predicted by general relativity on these astronomical length-scales.<ref>{{cite news|title=Einstein proved right in another galaxy|url=http://uopnews.port.ac.uk/2018/06/22/einstein-proved-right-in-another-galaxy/|date=22 June 2018|access-date=28 July 2018|publisher=University of Portsmouth|work=Press Office}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=A precise extragalactic test of General Relativity|author=Thomas E. Collett |display-authors=etal |journal=Science|volume=360|issue=6395|pages=1342–1346|date=22 June 2018|doi=10.1126/science.aao2469|pmid=29930135 |arxiv=1806.08300|bibcode=2018Sci...360.1342C|s2cid=49363216 }}</ref>
